rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Definite proper nouns on أفعل are diptotes because they resemble verbs; they take tanwīn when indefinite, since indefiniteness is lighter.
rows.anchor: المعرفة لأن المعارف أثقل وانصرفت في النكرة لبعدها من الأفعال وتركوا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites أعصر among forms Arabs do not decline as definite names; one dialect likewise leaves يعصر uninflected, while indefinite forms take tanwīn because they are not adjectives.
rows.anchor: العرب يعصر لا يصرفونه أيضا وتصرف ذلك في النكرة لأنه ليس بصفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An initial alif or yāʾ in a four-letter noun is treated as augmented; their frequency in triliteral roots supports that analysis unless contrary evidence appears.
rows.anchor: هذه الياء والألف لا تقع واحدة منهما في أول اسم على أربعة أحرف إلا وهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The frequency of initial alif and yāʾ in triliteral roots supports treating them as augmentative.
rows.anchor: يدلك أنها زائدة كثرة دخولها في بنات الثلاثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Awlaq is analyzed with an extra wāw; absent evidence, the more common pattern would be أفعل.
rows.anchor: فإن أولقا إنما الزيادة فيه الواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names such as أكلل and أيقق take tanwīn because their doubled initial consonants could not fit أفعل.
rows.anchor: ولو جاء في الكلام شيء نحو أكلل وأيقق فسميت به رجلا صرفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أول is analyzed as أفعل, as shown by its comparative and feminine forms.
rows.anchor: هو أول منه ومررت بأول منك والأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: البب is diptotic because it derives from اللب and follows أفعل.
rows.anchor: لأنه من اللب وهو أفعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A line is cited to show the connection of البب to لبّه.
rows.anchor: قد علت ذاك بنات ألببه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An initial consonant in a verb-like pattern is counted as augmentative only with evidence; تنضب supports tāʾ as extra.
rows.anchor: لا يجعل الحرف الأول منه زائدا إلا بثبت نحو تنصب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ترتب may be left without tanwīn, but those who decline it treat its augmented initial as having escaped resemblance to verbs.
rows.anchor: ومن قال ترتب صرف لأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تدرأ derives from درأت, and the form التتفل is supported by Arab pronunciation.
rows.anchor: وكذلك التدرأ إنما هو من درأت وكذلك التتفل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name تألب follows تفعّل and is linked to ألب يألب, said of a donkey driving or pursuing.
rows.anchor: وكذلك رجل يسمى تألب لأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Names like نهشل and تولب are declined as their initial nūn or tāʾ is treated as original absent evidence of augmentation.
rows.anchor: وأما ما جاء نحو نهشل وتولب فهو عندنا من نفس الحرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh says al-Khalīl and Yūnus also regard nūn and tāʾ as less frequently augmentative than alif and yāʾ, so names like نهشل remain declinable.
rows.anchor: والنون في الزيادة ليست كحال الألف والياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh attributes to al-Khalīl and Yūnus the view that names إثمِد, إصبع, and أبلم are diptotes because they resemble imperatives.
rows.anchor: وإذا سميت رجلا بإثمد لم تصرفه لأنه يشبه إضرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nouns rarely begin with augmentative prefixes on verb patterns, so such names resist tanwīn; Afعل is especially common among adjectives because adjectives resemble verbs.
rows.anchor: ليس أصل الأسماء عندهم على أن تكون في أولها الزوائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name on يَفْعَل with an augmented initial, such as يزيد or يشكر, is especially deserving of diptote treatment; forms in the chapter take tanwīn when indefinite.
rows.anchor: وهذا النحو أحرى أن لا تصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أحمر takes tanwīn as an indefinite because it remains an adjective and returns to that state; يزيد was made a name while definite and does not revert in the same way.
rows.anchor: فإن قلت فما بالك تصرف يزيد في النكرة وإنما منعك من صرف أحمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A name taken from an imperative such as إضرب is diptotic, and its hamzat al-waṣl is cut so it becomes noun-like.
rows.anchor: وإذا سميت رجلا بإضرب أو أقتل أو إذهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: اسم and ابن are too rare to overturn the rule; امرئ remains declinable as a name because it transfers noun to noun and has forms unlike any verb.
rows.anchor: فإذا سميت بامرئ رجلا تركته على حاله لأنك نقلته من اسم إلى اسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Naming from انطلاق transfers noun to noun, so its hamzat al-waṣl is not cut.
rows.anchor: ولو سميته انطلاقا لم تقطع الألف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nouns with an augmented initial that do not follow a verb pattern are declinable, including إصليت and أسلوب; the same applies to formations derived from verbs such as يضروب and تضريب.
rows.anchor: فإنه مصروف وذلك نحو إصليت وأسلوب وينبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: هراق is diptotic because its hāʾ is treated like an extra alif; هرق is compared with اقم.
rows.anchor: وإن سميت رجلا هراق لم تصرفه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Diminutives can become diptotic through resemblance to other verb-like forms: تضيرب resembles تغلب, أجيدل resembles أميلح, and هريق is likewise uninflected.
rows.anchor: ثم حقرته فقلت تضيرب لم تصرفه لأنه يصير بمنزلة تغلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kāna-type construction requires its predicate; one cannot stop at the subject, just as ẓanantu requires its second object.
rows.anchor: الفاعل كما لم يجز في ظننت الاقتصار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāna, yakūnu, ṣāra, mā dāma, and laysa normally require a predicate to complete the clause.
rows.anchor: كان ويكون وصار ومادام وليس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kāna can also occur with only a subject meaning it came into being or occurred; dāma can mean persisted or remained.
rows.anchor: تقول قد كان عبد الله أي قد خلق عبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣbaḥa and amsā can mean either a state change like kāna or waking and sleeping.
rows.anchor: وكما يكون أصبح وأمسى مرة بمنزلة كان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Laysa has no subject-only use, so it cannot omit its predicate in that way.
rows.anchor: فأما ليس فإنه لا يكون فيها ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetic examples use kāna to mean وقع, with an understood day or event as subject.
rows.anchor: إذا كان يوم ذو كواكب أشهب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With one definite and one indefinite term, the definite normally serves as subject because both terms describe one referent known to the listener.
rows.anchor: فالذي تشغل به كان المعرفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The known subject can precede or follow its predicate without changing its semantic role; an indefinite subject first is avoided because it obscures the referent.
rows.anchor: كان زيد حليما وكان حليما زيد لا عليك أقدمت أم أخرت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An adjective can distinguish homonymous people, and questions likewise begin from a person already known to the listener.
rows.anchor: كان زيد الطويل منطلقا إذا خفت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poetry and weak usage may reverse the expected order because kāna behaves like a verb and context identifies the referent; examples are cited from Khudāsh, Ḥassān, Abū Qays, and al-Farazdaq.
rows.anchor: وذلك قول خداش بن زهير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For al-Farazdaq’s line, most transmitters read السكران accusative and the next term nominative by resumption; another version raises the first term.
rows.anchor: أكثرهم ينصب السكران ويرفع الآخر على قطع وابتداء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If both terms are definite, either can be the subject; the subject is nominative and the predicate accusative.
rows.anchor: وإذا كانا معرفة فأنت بالخيار أيهما ما جعلته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The case of من or أيهم distinguishes whether it is the subject or predicate, as in the parallel ḍaraba construction.
rows.anchor: وتقول من كان أخاك ومن كان أخوك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In an exclusive negative clause such as ما كان أخاك إلا زيد, the postposed name is the subject, parallel to the ḍaraba construction.
rows.anchor: ما كان أخاك إلا زيد

words: ما كان حجتهم إلا أن قالوا
وما كان جواب قومه إلا أن قالوا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sībawayh cites the Qur’anic exclusive clauses as examples of the same kāna construction and its case pattern.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك قوله عز وجل

words: ما كان حجتهم إلا أن قالوا
rows.speaker: بعض القراء
rows.claim: Some readers raised the first term instead, an alternative parsing of the cited exclusive construction.
rows.anchor: وقد قرأ بعض القراء ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom ما جاءت حاجتك means “what has become your need,” treating جاء like kāna and matching feminine حاجتك.
rows.anchor: ما صارت حاجتك ولكنه أدخل التأنيث على ما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In من كانت أمك feminine agreement follows the understood referent; جاء is treated like kāna only in this fixed proverb.
rows.anchor: من كانت أمك حيث أوقع من على مؤنث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb جاء is made equivalent to kāna only in this fixed proverb because it is an idiom.
rows.anchor: في هذا الحرف وحده لأنه بمنزلة المثل

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Most Arabs say ما جاءت حاجتك rather than ما جاء حاجتك; Yūnus says he heard Ruʾba use the expression.
rows.anchor: وزعم يونس أنه سمع رؤبة يقول ما جاءت حاجتك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feminine agreement can follow a feminine understood referent or a partitive phrase, as in the cited Qur’anic examples.
rows.anchor: إذ صارت تقع على مؤنث قراءة بعض القراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Partitive بعض can trigger feminine agreement when it denotes a portion of a feminine whole, but not with an unrelated masculine noun.
rows.anchor: ذهبت بعض أصابعه وإنما أنت البعض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets use feminine agreement with nouns whose understood referent or semantic relation is feminine; examples include al-Aʿshā and other poets.
rows.anchor: وتشرق بالقول الذي قد أذعته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A trusted Arab said اجتمعت أهل اليمامة, using feminine agreement because اليمامة means its people in the expression.
rows.anchor: اجتمعت أهل اليمامة لأنه يقول في كلامه اجتمعت اليمامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A man addressed as طلحة takes a masculine imperative despite the name’s feminine ending; Sībawayh relates this to common truncation in address.
rows.anchor: بالترخيم فترك الحاء على حالها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: يا تيم تيم عدي أقبل is another poetic example of the same address and agreement pattern.
rows.anchor: يا تيم تيم عدى لا أبالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine marker is omitted in these constructions, though retaining it is also good in many such cases.
rows.anchor: وترك التاء في جميع هذا الحد والوجه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Feminine agreement is not licensed merely by a nearby feminine noun: عبد أمك is not part of or belonging to the mother.
rows.anchor: من ضربت عبد أمك أو هذه عبد زينب لم يجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Place expressions are accusative because they denote where something is located or occurs; an element before or after them governs them.
rows.anchor: وذاك لأنها ظروف فيها الأشياء وتكون فيها فانتصب لأنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Locative expressions include خلفك, قدامك, أمامك, تحتك, قبالتك, and ناحية الدار.
rows.anchor: فالمكان قولك هو خلفك وهو قدامك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: شرقي حوران and اليمينا are locative accusatives meaning east of and on the right side; Sībawayh cites Jarīr and ʿAmr ibn Kulthūm.
rows.anchor: هبت جنوبا فذكرى ما ذكرتكم

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus transmits from Abū ʿAmr the interpretation of مجراها اليمينا as “on the right side,” and says it is Abū ʿAmr’s own view.
rows.anchor: حدثنا بذلك يونس عن أبى عمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قصدك means “in your direction”; a line about the Pleiades and a report from reliable Arabs support this sense.
rows.anchor: يقال هو حلة الغور أى قصده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: جنابتا الأنف means the two lines flanking a gazelle’s nose; al-Aʿshā’s phrase جنبى فطيمة is parallel evidence for the two sides.
rows.anchor: خطان جنابتى أنفها يعنى الخطين اللذين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Locatives are accusative in the same structural way as measure expressions such as عشرين درهما and a quality complement such as عملا.
rows.anchor: هو غيره وصار بمنزلة المنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The locative is governed by the place or predicate associated with it, paralleling the relation between subject and predicate.
rows.anchor: والعامل فى خلف الذى هو موضع له والذى هو فى موضع خبره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: مكان فلان can mean “in his place,” namely a substitute who replaces him and performs his role.
rows.anchor: أى معى رجل يكون بدلا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Expressions such as خلفك, مكانك, and صددك share one underlying accusative construction.
rows.anchor: ومثل ذلك هو صددك وهو سقبك وهو قربك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Locative forms can also function as nouns rather than adverbs; Labīd’s verse uses خلفها and أمامها as names of the sides.
rows.anchor: أسماء غير ظروف بمنزلة زيد وعمرو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سواءك means “your substitute” like مكانك; it occurs as a noun in poetry.
rows.anchor: إذا جعلته فى معنى بدلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كعبد الله means “in a state like ʿAbd Allāh”; poets may use ك as مثل under poetic necessity.
rows.anchor: أى أنت فى حال كعبد الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ability to take مِن or على, as in بمن سواءك, supports treating these expressions as locative-like; ordinary adjectives do not fit the same pattern.
rows.anchor: بمنزلة الظروف أنك تقول مررت بمن سواءك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: أقبل قبلك means the caravan approaches your direction, while نحى نحوك means it is directed toward your side.
rows.anchor: وتقول كيف أنت إذا أقبل قبلك ونحى نحوك

rows.speaker: الخليل
rows.claim: Al-Khalīl accepts accusative قريب when it is treated as a locative, meaning a place near you.
rows.anchor: وزعم الخليل رحمه الله ~~أن النصب جيد إذا جعله ظرفا

rows.speaker: يونس
rows.claim: Yūnus reports Arabs saying هل قريبا منك أحد, parallel to هل قربك أحد.
rows.anchor: حدثنا يونس أن العرب تقول فى كلامها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: دونك is not raised in its ordinary locative use; the source treats it as an extended comparison or substitution expression.
rows.anchor: وأما دونك فإنه لا يرفع أبدا وإن قلت هو دونك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The original sense of locatives is an earthly place or settled location, extended in expressions like لصلب القناة and لمن شجرة صالحة.
rows.anchor: ولكنه جاز هذا كما تقول إنه لصلب القناة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قصد قصدك behaves like نحى نحوك and أقبل قبلك and can be nominative or accusative; دون alone can also mean inferior.
rows.anchor: وأما قصد قصدك فمثل نحى نحوك وأقبل قبلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bare جوف, داخل, and خارج do not function as adverbs; they require في or من, unlike خلف and similar terms.
rows.anchor: فمما لا يحسن أن يكون ظرفا أن العرب لا تقول هو جوف المسجد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: خلف and related terms denote sides around a noun, so they can become adverbs or nouns; جوف and داخل instead resemble body-part terms.
rows.anchor: وإنما فرق بين خلف وما أشبهها وبين هذه الحروف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: وسط الدار can be an adverb, but وسطه is a noun as shown by its direct-object use; في وسط الدار is a prepositional nominal phrase.
rows.anchor: ويدلك على أن المجرور بمنزلة الاسم غير الظرف أنك تقول زيد وسط الدار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قبل, قصد, and ناحية more readily function as nouns than خلف, أمام, and تحت, though the latter usage is attested.
rows.anchor: واعلم أن الظروف بعضها أشد تمكنا من بعض فى الأسماء نحو القبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rare locative terms include صددك for direction, سقبك for nearness, وزن الجبل for a side, and زنة الجبل for opposite.
rows.anchor: صددك ومعناه القصد وسقبك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: قرابتك في العلم means “close to you in knowledge”; حذاءه and إزاءه mean facing him, while حوالية and أقطار describe surrounding regions.
rows.anchor: ومن ذلك قول العرب هم قرابتك أى قربك يعنى المكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayya al-Numayrī’s مساليه means the two sides or flanks, paralleling جنبى فطيمة.
rows.anchor: إذا ما نعشناه على الرحل ينثنى
